summary: Adapts SDP to express one or more source addresses as a source filter for destination connection addresses. It defines a source-filter attribute that can list IPv4 or IPv6 addresses as an inclusion or exclusion list. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: When you subscribe to a broadcast, you can say only listen to these senders or ignore those. This lets the call's info card say exactly that.

subtitle: An SDP attribute that lists which sender addresses a receiver should accept, or ignore, for a session.

tldr.problem: A session description names where traffic is sent but not who is allowed to send it, so receivers cannot tell legitimate senders from illegitimate ones.
tldr.mechanism: The source-filter attribute is written as a=source-filter: followed by incl or excl, a network type, an address type, a destination address and a list of source addresses. Receivers accept only listed sources for incl, or reject listed sources for excl.
tldr.outcome: It can describe a Source-Specific Multicast session, but source addresses are weak authentication, so it must not be a receiver's only protection.

today: RFC 4570 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the SDP specification in RFC 4566.

sections.title: Why Filter Sources
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) is a text format that describes a multimedia session. It is not a protocol itself and can be carried by SAP, SIP, RTSP, email or HTTP. A description usually names an IP multicast address as the connection-address, the destination, though unicast addresses or fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) may also be used.

The source-filter attribute adds the addresses of legitimate senders. Receivers use the source and destination pair to discard traffic from illegitimate senders. They may also share the information with network elements such as routers using IGMPv3, so filtering can happen closer to the source. The goal is to protect receivers, preserve content integrity and help against Denial of Service attacks. The attribute may appear at session level, media level or both.
sections.eli5: When many people can send messages to the same place, you want a way to say which senders you trust. The source filter is that list.

sections.title: The source-filter Attribute
sections.content:
The syntax is a=source-filter: <filter-mode> <filter-spec>. The attribute does not change any existing SDP syntax or semantics.

  • filter-mode is incl or excl. With incl a packet is accepted only if its source is in the list. With excl a packet is rejected if its source is in the list.
  • nettype is the network type, mainly IN for the Internet.
  • address-types is IP4 or IP6, or * when the destination is an FQDN, since DNS can return either type.
  • dest-address must match one of the session's connection addresses. It may be unicast, multicast, an FQDN, or * to match all of them.
  • src-list is one or more unicast addresses or FQDNs separated by spaces.

The addresses are those seen by the receiver. If NAT or tunneling changes source addresses on the way, the attribute is only accurate if the addresses in it are translated too.
sections.eli5: The line says whether it is a list of allowed senders or blocked senders, where the messages are going, and then names the senders.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
The dest-address must match an existing connection field, unless * is used. For a multicast destination it must not include the ttl or number-of-addresses parts. If a connection field covers several multicast addresses, each needs its own a=source-filter line unless * is used. When the address type is *, the destination must be an FQDN or *, not an IP address.

With no source-filter, traffic from any source is accepted. The grammar has no way to say "exclude none" or "include all". A media-level filter always completely overrides a session-level one, and a filter need not sit at the same level as its connection field. A description must not contain more than one session-level filter covering the same destination address, or more than one media-level filter covering the same destination address. There is no limit on the number of entries in the source list, but practical limits such as session description size should be considered.
sections.eli5: If there is no list, everyone is let in. If a list is given for one part of the call, it replaces the list for the whole call. Each address may only have one list at each level.

sections.title: Examples and Offer-Answer Use
sections.content:
In the Source-Specific Multicast example, c=IN IP4 232.3.4.5/127 and a=source-filter: incl IN IP4 232.3.4.5 192.0.2.10 mean that only traffic from 192.0.2.10 to that group is accepted. For an RTP session, an incl filter also applies to RTCP, so only Sender Reports from that source could be multicast. The RFC says such a description SHOULD also include an a=rtcp-unicast attribute so Reception Reports are sent by unicast.

Other examples show an exclusion filter on a unicast destination, a * destination that covers two multicast addresses, a connection field with three multicast addresses where only two get filters, an IPv6 pair, and FQDNs with * as the address type.

The attribute is not meant as an offer in an SDP offer-answer exchange, because source sets are not capabilities of the offerer. An answerer may include it, for example to designate an SSM session, but SHOULD ignore any source-filter in the original offer.
sections.eli5: The examples show a list that allows only one sender into a group, a list that blocks one sender, and lists that cover several groups at once.

sections.title: Fit With Any-Source Multicast
sections.content: Listing legitimate sources departs from the Any-Source Multicast (ASM) model, which supports anonymous senders and all kinds of multicast applications. A source filter excludes some unknown or undesirable senders, which suits one-to-many or few-to-few applications better. The RFC says the two models can coexist on the same network using the same protocols, and that source filters do not corrupt ASM semantics but give receivers more control at their discretion.
sections.eli5: Normally anyone can talk to a group. A guest list is an extra choice a listener can make for themselves, and it does not break the normal way things work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The central question is whether addresses are authentic. Using a source IP address for authentication is weak, since addresses are often assigned dynamically and a sender can spoof its source address. Border routers are encouraged to drop datagrams with invalid source addresses, but this does not stop spoofing on a LAN.

NAT or tunneling may force translation of the addresses in the attribute and may collapse many original sources into a smaller set. FQDNs add flexibility but expose the filter to DNS weaknesses, since an unsecured DNS server could return illegitimate addresses. If the filter is shared with network elements, the security of that protocol, such as IGMPv3, also matters. For these reasons receivers SHOULD NOT treat the source-filter as their sole mechanism for protecting the integrity of received content.
sections.eli5: A sender can pretend to be someone else, so the guest list cannot be your only guard. It helps, but you should use other protections too.

data.code:
c=IN IP4 232.3.4.5/127
a=source-filter: incl IN IP4 232.3.4.5 192.0.2.10
